passage: At the small cooperative bank branch in Nabha, Amandeep watched how Nilesh worked. When the regional manager visited, Nilesh was all smiles and stories, presenting the new farmer-loan filing system as his own. Amandeep and the two clerks had built it over the monsoon, while Nilesh called their work "just typing". The clerks grumbled in the back room, and one stopped staying late. Amandeep didn't rant or try to out-charm him. That evening she took out the register where she had logged every change with dates and names, and wrote a short, plain note to the manager listing who had done which part. At the next meeting she asked that each clerk present their own section.

qa.q: When did Amandeep and the clerks build the filing system?
qa.a: They built it over the monsoon.

qa.q: What might the clerk who stopped staying late be feeling?
qa.a: The clerk probably feels unappreciated and discouraged after Nilesh called their work "just typing".

qa.q: What choice did Amandeep make instead of ranting, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She used her dated register to write a plain note on who did what and asked each clerk to present, keeping to facts and protecting morale.

qa.q: How might the regional manager see things after reading Amandeep's note?
qa.a: The manager would likely get a clearer, fairer picture of the work than Nilesh's charm gave.

grounding: A bank officer sees a colleague take credit and belittle others while charming seniors, and answers with records and facts rather than competition.

passage: At the NGO office in Nairobi, Priscila watched it happen again in Monday's meeting. Wanjiru presented the school-meals survey to the director as "my analysis", though Priscila and two interns had coded every form. Later, by the kettle, Wanjiru called one intern's charts "a bit amateur", loud enough for everyone to hear. Priscila felt heat in her chest, and the urge to go straight to the director and outshine Wanjiru. She didn't. That evening she opened a shared document and started listing who did what, with dates and file links. On Wednesday she sent a short, factual email to the team and the director: "Summary of survey contributions attached, for the report credits." She didn't add a single adjective.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru call the intern's charts?
qa.a: "a bit amateur"

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling after the meeting?
qa.a: She felt angry, with heat in her chest, and tempted to compete for the director's admiration.

qa.q: Why was Priscila's email a wise response?
qa.a: It relied on records and facts, protecting the team's credit without a fight for attention.

qa.q: How might the intern feel after hearing the charts called amateur?
qa.a: The intern probably felt embarrassed and discouraged, especially in front of others.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees credit-taking and belittling, then keeps records and addresses it factually.

passage: In the staff room of the Aizawl higher secondary school, Lalremsiami listened as Madhav told the principal about "his" science exhibition: the stalls, the judges, the parents' praise. She had drawn up the timetable; the lab assistant had built the stands; three teachers had stayed till nine. Madhav thanked no one. When the young computer teacher suggested an online sign-up for next year, Madhav laughed. "Leave the planning to people with experience." Lalremsiami noticed how the principal beamed at him. She kept her voice level. "Sir, I've made a short note of who handled each part, so we can plan next year. I'll email it to everyone." The note was just a table. The principal read it that evening and, next morning, thanked the lab assistant by name.

qa.q: Who built the stands?
qa.a: The lab assistant.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as Madhav took the credit?
qa.a: She was frustrated and concerned for the team, but stayed calm and kept her voice level.

qa.q: Which choice of Lalremsiami's worked, and why?
qa.a: A plain table of who did what, because it put the facts in front of the principal without competing for praise.

qa.q: What is it like for the young computer teacher when Madhav laughs at the idea?
qa.a: The young computer teacher likely feels belittled and less willing to share ideas.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who sees credit-taking and belittling, records contributions and addresses them factually.

passage:
Dear Bhupen,
You said to write if work got tricky, so here I am. Our new colleague, Karan, is charming with the seniors and awful with the rest of us. Last week he presented the vendor comparison I built as his own, and in the team call he called our intern's slides "school-level". My first instinct was to fight him for the spotlight. Then I remembered what you used to say: keep records, keep calm. So I've started a simple log of who does what, with dates. On Friday I told our manager just the facts: "The vendor sheet was mine; the version history shows it." She thanked me and changed the report credits. I'm still annoyed. But the team seems lighter.
Vinita

qa.q: What does the version history show?
qa.a: That the vendor sheet was Vinita's.

qa.q: What was Vinita's first instinct, and how does Vinita feel now?
qa.a: Vinita wanted to fight for the spotlight, and still feels annoyed, but calmer after using facts.

qa.q: What approach did Vinita take that protected the work?
qa.a: Keeping a dated log of contributions and telling the manager only the facts.

qa.q: How might the intern feel after Karan's "school-level" comment?
qa.a: The intern was likely embarrassed and discouraged by the public put-down.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices credit-taking and belittling, keeps records and raises it factually instead of competing.

passage:
Okay, so you want to know how I handled Bidisha? I'm Leela, I work on the data team, and this went on for six months.
In meetings with the directors, Bidisha was warm and funny. Back at our desks, she'd say things like, "Leela's slides are cute, I'll fix them." Then she'd present my analysis as her own.
At first I was furious and wanted to outshine her in front of the bosses. That would have turned it into a contest.
Instead I started keeping records: dated emails, file histories, who did which chart. When she presented my forecast, I said calmly in the meeting, "Happy to walk through the method, since I built the model." I didn't insult her. Just the facts.
My manager checked the files. Credit got corrected. The rest of the team started doing the same, and the mood got better.

qa.q: What records did Leela start keeping?
qa.a: Dated emails, file histories, and who did which chart.

qa.q: How did Leela first feel about Bidisha taking credit?
qa.a: Leela was furious at first and wanted to outshine Bidisha in front of the bosses.

qa.q: Why was Leela's factual approach better than competing?
qa.a: It kept the focus on the work and the evidence rather than a popularity contest, so credit was corrected and team morale improved.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Leela offered to explain the method?
qa.a: Bidisha may have felt caught out and embarrassed in front of the directors, since the calm facts showed who built the model.

grounding: Shows a colleague observing a co-worker's credit-taking and responding with records and calm facts rather than competing for admiration.
